summary: Describes how to send IPv4 and IPv6 packets over Ethernet in access networks that use IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) radio. The Ethernet is realized by bridging connections the 802.16 network provides between a base station and its clients. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A wireless broadband tower can act like a long network cable to each customer. This document explains how ordinary Internet traffic rides over that wireless link by pretending it is regular Ethernet.

subtitle: How to run ordinary IPv4 and IPv6 over a WiMAX-style radio network by making it look like Ethernet.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 radio links are connection-oriented and point-to-multipoint, with no native two-way broadcast or multicast, yet IP expects Ethernet-like behavior.
tldr.mechanism: Each subscriber station's radio connections are bridged by a network-side bridging function, so the access network looks like switched Ethernet. Broadcast and multicast are replicated over unicast, and IP-aware tricks such as Proxy ARP keep traffic off the air.
tldr.outcome: Hosts follow the normal IPv4-over-Ethernet and IPv6-over-Ethernet rules, with a default MTU of 1500 bytes, while the bridge saves scarce radio resources.

today: RFC 5692 is a Proposed Standard from October 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Ethernet on a Radio Network
sections.content:
RFC 5692 describes how to carry IPv4 and IPv6 over Ethernet in an access network built on IEEE 802.16, a fixed-to-mobile broadband wireless system. IEEE 802.16 offers a packet convergence sublayer (CS) with an Ethernet-specific part, and a generic packet CS (GPCS). This document covers both.

Ethernet was designed for a shared medium, while 802.16 is point-to-multipoint like other cellular systems. So Ethernet is realized by bridging the radio connections between a base station (BS) and its subscriber stations (SS).

Because radio resources are scarce, the RFC adds IP-specific support functions in the Ethernet layer above 802.16 while keeping full compatibility with standard IP over Ethernet behavior.
sections.eli5: Imagine a tower talking to many houses by radio, but your computer expects a plain network cable. This document is the translator that makes the radio link behave like that cable.

sections.title: The IEEE 802.16 Link Model
sections.content:
The 802.16 MAC sets up connections between a BS and each SS. Each connection is one service flow with its own QoS profile and is identified by a 16-bit Connection Identifier (CID). Several connections, each with its own QoS class and direction, can exist between a BS and one SS.

Although the BS and every SS have unique 48-bit MAC addresses, packets over the air are identified only by the CID in the 802.16 MAC header. This lets arbitrary source and destination MAC addresses in Ethernet frames cross the link, which is needed when an SS sits behind a bridge attached to another network. The BS can bundle all unicast connections of one SS into a single layer-2 link on the network side.

802.16 does not support bidirectional native broadcast and multicast for IP. Downlink connections can multicast to a group of SSs, but uplink connections are unicast only. The RFC also notes that Multicast and Broadcast Service (MBS) is invisible to the IP layer, so it does not carry IP broadcast or multicast data.
sections.eli5: Each house gets its own private channel to the tower, labeled with a number. Shouting to everyone at once does not work well on these channels, so the tower has to talk to each house one at a time.

sections.title: The Ethernet Link Model and the Bridge
sections.content:
All point-to-point connections belonging to an SS MUST be connected to a network-side bridging function, much like hosts plugged into a switch. This can be one centralized bridge or several interconnected bridges, preferably in a hierarchy. The BS MUST forward all service flows of one SS to one bridge port, and no more than one SS may be connected to a given port. If several end stations sit behind an SS, the SS SHOULD act as a subscriber-side bridge according to 802.1D and 802.16k.

The bridging function MUST create a radio-side port when a new SS attaches and remove it when the SS detaches. It MUST be based on 802.1D and its amendment 802.16k. Extra IP-specific functions MAY be added to avoid flooding broadcast or multicast packets.

Since 802.16 defines no Ethernet broadcast or multicast, such frames SHOULD be replicated and sent over unicast connections, with the bridge doing the copying. The bridge MAY also support VLANs according to 802.1Q to shrink the broadcast domain, with each VLAN representing an IP link.
sections.eli5: The bridge is like a school secretary. Every classroom has its own phone line to the office, and when there is an announcement for everyone the secretary calls each room separately.

sections.title: Carrying IPv4 and IPv6 Packets
sections.content:
Hosts sending IPv4 over Ethernet over 802.16 MUST follow RFC 894. Addresses can be configured by hand or via DHCPv4, and the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) MUST be used to find the destination MAC address.

Hosts sending IPv6 MUST follow RFC 2464. Router discovery relies on Router Advertisements, but periodic ones waste radio resources and disturb dormant-mode stations, so AdvDefaultLifetime and MaxRtrAdvInterval SHOULD be overridden with the high values given in Section 8.3 of RFC 5121. Stateful configuration MUST use DHCPv6, stateless configuration MUST use the mechanisms of RFC 4862 and RFC 4861, and Neighbor Discovery MUST be used for address resolution.

The default MTU for both IPv4 and IPv6 packets on the link MUST be 1500 bytes. The same IPv4 prefix and the same set of IPv6 prefixes MAY be assigned to all hosts on the link, which places them on the same subnetwork.
sections.eli5: Once the radio link pretends to be Ethernet, computers use their usual rules to find each other and get addresses. The only change is to talk less often, so the radio is not kept busy.

sections.title: Saving Radio Resources
sections.content:
An ordinary bridge floods broadcasts out of every port, which is wasteful on a radio network with dormant-mode hosts. The bridge SHOULD prevent broadcasting to all radio-side ports and can handle multicast control messages according to RFC 4541, forwarding multicast data only to ports suitable for the group.

For DHCPv4, the bridge SHOULD filter broadcast DHCPOFFER and DHCPACK messages and forward them only to the host named in the chaddr field. Alternatively, DHCP Relay Agent Information (option 82) MAY be used, with the bridge port number as Circuit ID.

For ARP, the bridge uses Proxy ARP to avoid broadcasting requests over the air. It SHOULD keep an ARP cache big enough for all its SSs, answer a request with a unicast ARP Reply if the target is cached, discard a request when the target is behind the same subscriber-side bridge, and silently discard any self-ARP Request. IPv6 Neighbor Solicitations go to the solicited-node multicast address and are handled as multicast.
sections.eli5: Instead of yelling a question to the whole neighborhood, the bridge keeps an address book and answers for you. That way the radio stays quiet and sleeping devices are not woken up.

sections.title: Public Access Networks
sections.content:
In a public access scenario, direct communication between nodes is restricted for security and accounting reasons. The access router (AR) is attached to a network-side bridge and MAY filter, police and account for all host traffic, like a Network Access Server (NAS).

If the AR acts as the NAS, all traffic from SSs SHOULD go to the AR, even between SSs served by the same AR. The bridge SHOULD forward upstream traffic toward the AR but MUST perform normal bridging for downstream traffic and MUST bridge SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) messages.

For IPv4, MAC-Forced Forwarding (RFC 4562) can answer ARP requests with the AR's MAC address. For IPv6, either a unique prefix per SS can be assigned, forcing traffic through the AR, or a common prefix can be used, in which case the Prefix Information Option SHOULD be advertised with the On-link flag reset.
sections.eli5: In a public network, everybody's mail goes through one front desk first. The desk can check it and keep count before passing it on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it introduces no new vulnerabilities to IPv4 and IPv6. Security of the 802.16 air interface, including admission control and ciphering, is the subject of the IEEE standard. A Traffic Encryption Key (TEK) is generated by the SS and BS after successful mutual authentication.

The bridged model keeps SSs from messaging each other without passing through the bridge, but it is still open to attacks known for bridged Ethernet, such as malicious reconfiguration of the bridge's address table during learning. Link security per 802.1AE can be layered on top, and SEND can secure neighbor discovery in the public access case.
sections.eli5: The radio link already locks its messages, and the bridge has the same weak spots any normal switch has. Extra locks can be added if needed.

viz.caption: HOW THE BRIDGE AVOIDS FLOODING THE AIR

items.title: Broadcast
items.text: Not flooded to all radio-side ports, except ARP, DHCPv4 and IGMP traffic handled by their own rules.

items.title: Multicast
items.text: Snooped per RFC 4541 and sent only to ports suitable for the group.

items.title: ARP
items.text: Proxy ARP answers from a cache with a unicast reply.

items.title: DHCPv4
items.text: Broadcast replies forwarded only to the host in chaddr.
